rows.item: Translation as transferring or conveying meaning (“principles = foundations”); defined as “an activity / process of transferring textual meaning from one language to another language”
rows.where: Chapter 1, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 1
rows.note: The definition is quoted and credited to the Translation Team’s course materials, and the lesson is put as “translation carries meaning, not words”.

rows.item: Arabic as a derivational language and English as a compounding language
rows.note: Stated in one line only, and not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Aims of the course: process versus product, basic rules and principles, differences, difficulties, strategies and techniques
rows.note: Turned into the list of what readers should be able to do by the end; the process-versus-product point was left out.

rows.item: Two characteristics of a translator: bilingual knowledge, and cultural knowledge equal to linguistic knowledge
rows.note: Rewritten as a short list: knows both languages and both cultures well.

rows.item: The process of translating: break a paragraph into sentences, sentences into phrases and phrases into words; keep the links such as cause and effect
rows.note: Kept as a working habit: break the text into pieces, work out each piece, then rebuild it.

rows.item: Text defined as anything written (a word, a sentence or a paragraph); to analyse a text means to break it down and process it
rows.note: The text definition was widened to any written or spoken piece of language, and analysis is now “breaking down and studying a text before translating it”.

rows.item: Main concepts of Translation Studies: equivalence (formal, functional, ideational) as a central concept
rows.note: Developed into a full chapter, with the three types explained by examples.

rows.item: Abbreviations TS, SL and TL with their Arabic terms ({{علم دراسات الترجمة}}, {{لغة المصدر}}, {{لغة الهدف}}); SLC (source language culture) and TLC (target language culture)
rows.note: Arabic wording adjusted to {{دراسات الترجمة}}, {{اللغة المصدر}} and {{اللغة الهدف}}, and the Arabic terms for SLC and TLC added.

rows.item: Small vocabulary items: loose = {{فضفاض}}; semantics = {{علم المعاني}} / {{علم الدلالة}}; the rule of adding “s” to semantics and linguistics; NGOs = non-governmental organisations
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: A second definition of translation: an approximation process, mostly of cultural meaning
rows.where: Chapter 1, Step 2; Words to remember, Chapter 1
rows.note: Kept with the reminder that an exact match is impossible; cultural meaning has its own chapter (Chapter 15).

rows.item: Two further ideas named without explanation: translation as “politicising” (diplomacy, asking a father for money) and relevance
rows.note: The notes name them without a full explanation.

rows.item: Form and meaning as a pair; the rule that meaning matters more than form ({{المعنى أهم من البناء}}); behind any form there is meaning; you may change the form but not the meaning; form can be a clause, sentence, paragraph, text, word structure, preposition or compound
rows.where: Chapter 5, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 5
rows.note: The Arabic word for form is now {{الشكل}} instead of {{البناء}}, and the list of forms is shortened to word, phrase, clause, sentence or text.

rows.item: Intralingual versus interlingual communication; communication as understanding and being understood; the six elements (sender, receiver, channel, message, perceived value, noise)
rows.note: Left out as too technical; Chapter 1, Step 3 only mentions that rewording in the same language is a wider kind of translation.

rows.item: Product cannibalism: literal meaning versus the cultural meaning of one product competing with another
rows.note: Spelled “cannibalisation” and defined as a new product taking sales from another product of the same company.

rows.item: Pay attention to the context; “every communicative situation has its own context” ({{لكل مقام مقال}})
rows.note: Kept as the saying that every situation has its own way of speaking.

rows.item: Two side remarks: dichotomy explained as a two-way split ({{التفرع الثنائي}}, “di” means two), and “meaning is complex because it is cognitive”
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Structural adjustment: the same meaning can be carried by a different form, for example an adjective changed into a verb, or a verb into a noun
rows.note: Shown with a noun-to-verb example, and later named “transposition”.

rows.item: Blair as Bush’s “puppy”: {{منقاد لبوش}}, {{تابع لبوش}} or a word such as “sheep”
rows.note: The animal is now “poodle”, the sheep suggestion was dropped, and the lesson is that the image changes while the meaning stays.

rows.item: Denotation (the core meaning of a word) and connotation (the shades of meaning added to it), with the Arabic labels {{المعنى اللغوي}} / {{المعنى الحرفي}} and {{المعنى اصطلاحاً}}
rows.where: Chapter 6, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 6
rows.note: Reworded in simpler words, and the Arabic labels became {{المعنى المعجمي}} and {{المعنى الإيحائي}}, because the notes use {{الاصطلاحي}} for idiomatic meaning too.

rows.item: Key vocabulary: translation = {{الترجمة التحريرية}}; interpretation = {{الترجمة الشفهية}}
rows.note: Kept as the two basic terms, with “interpretation” changed to “interpreting”.

rows.item: Legal vocabulary: provided that = {{شريطة أن}} / {{بشرط}}; Article 12, Governing Law = {{القانون المطبق}} (not {{القانون الحاكم}}); article = {{المادة}} in a constitution, {{البند}} in an agreement
rows.note: Put into a sample term list, with {{القانون الواجب التطبيق}} first and {{القانون الحاكم}} shown as a common calque instead of a mistake.

rows.item: Died = {{قتل}} (denotation) and died = {{استشهد}} (connotation); kill versus assassinated
rows.note: The Arabic glosses were unclear ({{قتل}} means “killed”), and the handbook uses other examples.

rows.item: Same meaning, different feeling: die, pass away and kick the bucket; steed = {{جواد}}, horse = {{حصان}}, mule = {{بغل}}; comrade ({{رفيق}}, same party) versus friend ({{صديق}})
rows.note: The dying words are described as neutral, polite and respectful, and informal and humorous (with {{مات}} and {{تُوُفِّي}} added), and mule was left out for space.

rows.item: Sentence meaning versus speaker’s meaning: {{أشعر بالحر}} means “turn on the air conditioning”; {{أصبح الجو بارداً}} means “turn it off”
rows.where: Chapter 6, Step 2; Words to remember, Chapter 6
rows.note: Made polite (“Please turn on the air conditioning”), and _It’s freezing in here_ was added.

rows.item: Collocation defined as “the company a word keeps”; pay money, pay attention, pay respect, pay a visit
rows.where: Chapter 8, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 8
rows.note: The definition is quoted and credited to the course materials, and the Arabic is now {{ينتبه}} / {{يُعير انتباهه}}, {{يُبدي احتراماً}} and {{يقوم بزيارة}}.

rows.item: More collocations: close cooperation = {{تعاون وثيق}}, close friend = {{صديق مقرب}}; strong tea = {{شاي ثقيل}} (not {{شاي قوي}}); Arabic examples {{استل سيفه}} and {{يساورني القلق}}
rows.note: The English examples are kept as written, and the Arabic examples were given English equivalents (he drew his sword; I am worried).

rows.item: Idiom defined as an expression of more than one word whose total meaning is not the sum of its words; it cannot be translated word by word
rows.where: Chapter 9, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 9
rows.note: Reworded, with tips added on how to spot an idiom.

rows.item: Idioms: I am all ears = {{كلي آذان صاغية}}; It’s raining cats and dogs = {{تمطر بغزارة}}; over the moon = {{في قمة السعادة}}
rows.note: Kept in the list of English idioms.

rows.item: To pull one’s socks up = {{شمر عن ساعديه}}
rows.note: The English idiom was changed to “to roll up one’s sleeves”, which matches the Arabic.

rows.item: A piece of cake: {{سهل}} as an idiom, {{قطعة من الكعك}} when meant literally, depending on context
rows.note: Kept, with a birthday-party example for the literal meaning.

rows.item: Basic principle for English into Arabic: start with the verb (English is SVO, Arabic is VSO)
rows.note: Softened to a general tendency, because a sentence that starts with the subject is also correct Arabic.

rows.item: Exercise table: He is in bed = {{نائم}}; “as” = {{بصفتي ضابط}}, {{بصفتي مدير الشركة}}; Shops stay open = {{تظل}} / {{تبقى}}; eventually = {{في نهاية المطاف}}; to see the Roman ruins = {{لمشاهدة}} / {{لزيارة}} / {{لرؤية}}
rows.note: Kept with short explanations, and the Arabic endings corrected ({{بصفتي ضابطاً}}, {{بصفتي مديرَ الشركة}}).

rows.item: Nouns with no feminine form ({{قاضي}}, {{نائب}}, {{ضابط}}), because {{قاضية}} and {{نائبة}} mean something else
rows.note: Given as “fatal” and “calamity”, with a note that both words are now widely used for women.

rows.item: Exercise: boys are boys = {{الولد ولد لو أنه قاضي بلد}}
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Exercise: Business is business = {{العمل التجاري عمل تجاري}} or {{الشغل شغل}}
rows.note: Only the informal {{الشغل شغل}} is kept, and it is marked as informal.

rows.item: Equivalence defined as matching two languages at different levels; the three types: formal (keep the form, such as passive for passive), functional and ideational
rows.where: Chapter 10, Steps 1 and 3; Words to remember, Chapter 10
rows.note: Explained with one worked sentence, and presented as a framework rather than steps in a fixed order.

rows.item: The agreement remained a dead letter: formal {{حرفاً ميتاً}}, functional {{حبراً على ورق}}, ideational {{لم يتم تطبيق…}}; treaty = {{معاهدة}}, agreement = {{اتفاقية}}
rows.note: The ideational version was reworded as {{لم تُطبَّق الاتفاقية…}}, and a comment was added on each version.

rows.item: You should think outside the box (formal {{فكر خارج الصندوق}}; functional {{فكر بتفكير خلاق}}); Ali is second to none in writing poetry (functional {{لا يشق له غبار}}; ideational {{متميز}})
rows.note: The plain-meaning versions are labelled ideational ({{لا يُضاهى}} for the poetry sentence), and the formal box version is noted as now used in Arabic too.

rows.item: Context defined as background information that helps us understand the text; micro context (inside, co-text) versus macro context (outside), also listed among the pairs of opposites
rows.where: Chapter 7, Step 2; Words to remember, Chapter 7
rows.note: Reworded, and explained as looking “near” and then “far”.

rows.item: Macro context: author ({{أحمد شوقي}}, {{نزار قباني}}, {{محمود درويش}}), audience, translator (bilingual and bicultural), time and place, economic, social and historical circumstances; the translation triangle with the translator in the middle
rows.note: Kept as author (Qabbani and Darwish only), audience, time, place and background, with the triangle described in words.

rows.item: Homonymy (unrelated meanings) versus polysemy (related meanings)
rows.where: Chapter 7, Step 3; Words to remember, Chapter 7
rows.note: Kept, with the Arabic terms {{المشترك اللفظي}} and {{تعدّد المعنى}} added.

rows.item: Examples: {{عين}} (spy, eye, spring), {{تطهير}}, {{احتجاز}}, bank (financial institution, river bank), case (situation, issue, container); {{بناء}} (a building, a college)
rows.note: Kept with Arabic and English glosses, and a Try it question added; {{بناء}} and “cover of a mobile” were left out.

rows.item: Literal translation (also “modified literal translation”); it can be successful or destructive: play a role = {{يلعب دوراً}} works, pay a visit = {{يدفع زيارة}} fails; It has been a long day; the wedding advert (“biggest day”)
rows.where: Chapter 11, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 11
rows.note: Kept with the Arabic saying {{قد تكون الترجمة الحرفية ناجحة أو مدمّرة}}, and the wrong version of the advert now follows “biggest” with {{أكبر}}.

rows.item: Translator types: commissioned (a client asks you) and self-initiated (you choose the text)
rows.where: Chapter 1, Step 5; Words to remember, Chapter 1
rows.note: Explained with examples, and the Arabic terms {{مترجم بتكليف}} and {{مترجم بمبادرة ذاتية}} added.

rows.item: The client’s ideology: A suicide bomber killed 10 Israelis, {{انتحاري}} versus {{استشهادي}}
rows.note: Made neutral (“killed ten people”) and shown as two points of view, so the translator follows the client’s policy.

rows.item: Environmental and social terms: global warming = {{احترار أرضي}}; greenhouse effect = {{احتباس حراري}}; cancel culture = {{ثقافة الإلغاء}} (also {{ثقافة الاستبعاد}})
rows.note: Given as accepted terms, with {{الاحترار العالمي}} for global warming and only {{ثقافة الإلغاء}} for cancel culture.

rows.item: Exercise 16: Don’t put words on me = {{لا تتقول علي الأقاويل}}; to hit the sac = {{أن يأوي إلى الفراش}}; to break a leg = {{أن تكون محظوظاً}}
rows.note: English corrected (“in my mouth”, “sack”) and Arabic reworded ({{لا تتقوّل عليّ}}, {{أوى إلى فراشه}}, {{بالتوفيق!}}), with a word-by-word version of “break a leg” added as a warning.

rows.item: Exercise 16: Break the rules = {{خرق القواعد}} / {{مخالفة القواعد}} / {{تجاوز القواعد}}
rows.note: Not needed here; “break the law” is covered in Chapter 8, Step 3.

rows.item: Keywords: rhetoric = {{البلاغة}}, poetic = {{فصيح}} / {{جزل}}; poetry is very expressive; subjective ({{ذاتي}}) versus objective ({{موضوعي}}) table
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level; Chapter 12, Step 1 says only that poetry is rich in metaphors.

rows.item: Metaphor and figurative language; metaphor as using a word in a non-basic meaning ({{استعارة}}); metaphor versus simile (“she is a moon”, “she is beautiful like a moon”); My thoughts evaporate = {{تبخرت أفكاري}}
rows.where: Chapter 12, Steps 1 and 3; Words to remember, Chapter 12
rows.note: The simile example changed to “He is a lion” and “as brave as a lion”, and the evaporate example became “My hopes evaporated” = {{تبخّرت آمالي}}.

rows.item: Three rules for metaphors: shared, translate literally (she is a snake = {{إنها أفعى}}); not shared, use another image ({{إنها كالثعلب}}); otherwise give the basic meaning ({{خطيرة}}, {{خبيثة}}), the worst choice
rows.note: Kept as ordered steps; the fox example is really a simile, so it became a separate step with a new example, and the last step now uses “The news raised a few eyebrows”.

rows.item: Tip of the iceberg = {{غيض من فيض}} (negative), {{أول الغيث قطرة}} (positive), {{وما خفي أعظم}}
rows.note: {{غيضٌ من فيض}} and {{وما خفي كان أعظم}} are kept; {{أول الغيث قطرة}} was left out for space.

rows.item: My paper will see light next December = {{ورقتي البحثية سترى النور…}}; raises the brows = {{تُصدم}}
rows.note: The English was completed to “see the light of day”, and the eyebrows example now reads {{أثار الخبر استغراب بعضهم}}.

rows.item: Free translation (“ample freedom”, also loose translation; not only for literary works); some specialists see adaptation as a new text, not a translation
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 11; Chapter 11, Step 3
rows.note: Kept as definitions; the remark that it is not only for literary works was left out.

rows.item: Free translation examples: Going out can be risky; Appointing new employees; heavy rainfall; his parents are not happy
rows.note: Turned into a lesson on how free is too free, with the virus example softened to “a disease is spreading”.

rows.item: Arabicisation as a form of naturalisation; a loan-word made by sound ({{الاستعارة الصوتية}}), radio = {{الراديو}}
rows.where: Chapter 17, Step 2; Words to remember, Chapter 16
rows.note: Kept as transliteration and Arabicisation ({{التعريب}}), with {{النقل الصوتي}} as the Arabic term; the word “naturalisation” is not used.

rows.item: Terms ({{مصطلحات}}) convey a complex meaning (a concept); translators sometimes coin words; terms mark technical texts; every branch has its own terms
rows.where: Chapter 17, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapters 16 and 21
rows.note: Kept as: a term names a concept, and a translator may have to coin a word; the other points were left out.

rows.item: The Jordanian Academy of the Arabic Language and its 74 specialised fields
rows.note: The figure is not used; Chapter 21, Step 2 names the Arabic academies in general, including Amman (source of that mention not checked).

rows.item: Exercise 24: a greenish field = {{حقل مائل للخضرة}}
rows.note: Used only as an example of English endings with regular Arabic equivalents: greenish = {{مائل إلى الخضرة}}.

rows.item: Exercise 25: fast colour = {{لون ثابت}}; fast friend = {{صديق وفي}}; weak coffee = {{قهوة خفيفة}}; rough sea = {{بحر هائج}}; breach of the law, {{كسر القانون}} versus {{مخالفة القانون}}
rows.where: Chapter 8, Step 3; Chapter 3, Step 1; Chapter 23, Step 2
rows.note: Kept as written, except that the law example now says {{يخالف القانون}} is more natural than {{يكسر القانون}}; “a fast colour” is also the dictionary example in Chapter 3.

rows.item: Exercises 24 and 25, the remaining items: a readable book, a conceivable resolution, retrievable properties, an arguable issue, boyish behaviour, a feminist writer, laudable efforts, an unrealisable objective, the translatability of idioms; addled egg; plain = {{سادة}} / {{واضح}} / plains = {{سهول}}; cover news = publish news, not “cover”
rows.note: Left out for space.

rows.item: Exercise 26: {{هذه حديقة غناء}}; The thief escaped = {{لاذ اللص بالفرار}}; sounds great; {{يعد الطقس متقلب}}; a good wife; the copular verb (the auxiliary working as a main verb)
rows.note: Left out for space; the verb-first idea is in Chapter 4, Step 1 and the copula idea in Step 2.

rows.item: Exercise 28: sheriff = {{مأمور الشرطة}} / {{عمدة الشرطة}}; watchdog press versus lap-dog press = {{الصحافة المعارضة للحكومة}} versus {{المؤيدة للحكومة}}
rows.note: The Arabic changed to {{رئيس شرطة المقاطعة}}, {{الصحافة الرقابية}} and {{الصحافة الموالية}}.

rows.item: Exercise 28: sleep like a log = {{نام كنومة أهل الكهف}} / {{كالقتيل}} / {{كالميت}}
rows.note: Only {{نام كالقتيل}} is kept.

rows.item: Exercise 29: God willing = {{إن شاء الله}}; We are well = {{الحمد لله}}
rows.note: Kept, with {{بخير}} added for “very well”.

rows.item: Exercise 29: Sorry to hear your loss = {{تعيش انت، شعبان مات}}; Welcome, welcome, we have the pleasure of having you here = {{أهلاً أهلاً زارنا النبي}}
rows.note: The Arabic was replaced by common phrases ({{عظّم الله أجركم}}, {{البقية في حياتك}}, {{أهلاً وسهلاً، شرّفتمونا}}) instead of these lines from a novel.

rows.item: Keywords: substitutes = {{بدائل}}, lexical items; bereavement = {{موت أو أحزان العائلة}}, bereaved families = {{العائلات الثكلى}}
rows.note: Only {{ثكلى}} is kept, as a word with no single English equivalent (“a bereaved mother”).

rows.item: Cultural approximation defined as bringing the meaning of the source language as close as possible to the target language; it needs cultural knowledge of both
rows.where: Chapter 15, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 15
rows.note: Reworded and credited to Farghal & Shunnaq (1999/2011).

rows.item: I have got the test in the bag = {{الامتحان في جيبي}} (that is, guaranteed)
rows.note: Kept as the opening example, with a formal version {{النجاح في الامتحان مضمون}} added.

rows.item: As busy as a bee = {{زي أم العروس}}; Like mother, like daughter = {{اقلب الجرة على فمها تطلع البنت لأمها}}; Ali and Ahmed are cut from the same cloth = {{من نفس الطينة}}; scapegoating = {{كبش الفداء}} / {{حطها برقبتي}}
rows.note: The bee example is now {{نشيطٌ كالنحلة}}, a plain version {{البنتُ تُشبه أمَّها}} was added, the cloth example is {{من طينةٍ واحدة}}, and the scapegoat is {{كبش فداء}} without the dialect phrases.

rows.item: Jet lag = {{إعياء الطيران}}
rows.note: Used as a paraphrase example with {{الإرهاق الناتج عن فارق التوقيت}}.

rows.item: Titles: the Home Office (UK), the Chancellor of the Exchequer (UK), the Secretary of the Treasury (US), the Secretary of State (US)
rows.note: Corrected to {{وزارة الداخلية البريطانية}} (not {{وزير}}) and {{وزير الخزانة الأمريكي}}, with the country added to each title.

rows.item: Other cultural-approximation examples: Every jack must have his jill = {{لكل روح توأمه}}; What the hell are you talking = {{اتق الله يا شيخ}}; Calm down = {{وحدوا الله والمسامح كريم}}; Death is the great leveller = {{كل نفس ذائقة الموت}}; big sins = {{الكبائر}}; Minister of Foreign Affairs in Kuwait; House Managers at the Clinton impeachment trial; intern; scandal
rows.note: Left out for space.

rows.item: Descriptive translation: paraphrasing a source expression by describing its concept; first transliterate, then describe; put the description in brackets or a footnote
rows.where: Chapter 16, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 16
rows.note: Turned into three steps (transliterate, describe, describe only the first time) and credited to Farghal & Shunnaq (1999/2011).

rows.item: Examples: {{زكاة}} = compulsory charity in Islam; {{تيمم}} = making ablutions with earth; {{الحوقلة}}; {{البسملة}}; Ali has been sectioned
rows.note: Kept with more exact descriptions, and the basmala and hawqala given with the phrases they stand for.

rows.item: Further examples: {{التأريخ}}, {{القهقهة}}, {{القرقرة}}, Yin-Yang; psychology versus psychiatry; dust versus dirt
rows.note: Left out for space.

rows.item: Concept = complex meaning ({{مفهوم}})
rows.note: Rewritten as “an idea that a word or term stands for”.

rows.item: Lexical creation as coinage of new words in the target language for culture-specific items; why it matters (a gap in the target language); title “Lexical Creation – {{النحت المعجمي}}”
rows.where: Chapter 17, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 17
rows.note: The Arabic term is now {{التوليد المعجمي}}, and the idea is credited to Farghal & Shunnaq (1999/2011).

rows.item: Thanksgiving = {{عيد الشكر}}; shadow government = {{حكومة الظل}} (a literal translation that still counts as lexical creation)
rows.note: Kept as loan-translation (calque) examples.

rows.item: “To be lexicalised” = {{التعجيم}}, adding a new word to the dictionary officially
rows.note: The Arabic term is now {{المَعْجَمة}}.

rows.item: Types of lexical creation: neologism, loan translation (calque), transliteration, explanation, hybrid form (CD = {{دسك مدمج}})
rows.note: Kept as the five methods, with the CD example replaced by cybersecurity.

rows.item: Examples: smartphone = {{الهاتف الذكي}}; blog = {{مدونة}}; cyber security = {{الأمن السيبراني}}; green washing = {{التضليل البيئي}}
rows.note: Cybersecurity is shown as a hybrid form, blog is explained through {{دوّن}}, and greenwashing is defined.

rows.item: Atwah = {{عطوة}}, a three-month truce in Jordanian culture
rows.note: Described as a temporary truce in tribal customary law, for example in Jordan; the three months were left out.

rows.item: Wakf = {{وقف}} and Sukok = {{صكوك}} (transliteration plus a short explanation)
rows.where: Chapter 14, Step 4; Chapter 16, Try it; Chapter 17, Step 2
rows.note: Spelled “waqf” and “sukuk”, and each is given a short definition.

rows.item: Al-Istitaba = {{الاستتابة}} (“a kind of repentance / ultimatum”)
rows.note: The meaning is unclear in the notes.

rows.item: Other coinages: peace talk = {{المفاوضات}}; co-wife = {{الضرة}}; Valentine’s Day = {{عيد الحب}}; columnist; tribocracy, dictatocracy, puppycracy, patriocracy; subordination = {{تبعية}}; {{الخلوة الشرعية}}
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: To be in the red = {{مديون}}
rows.note: The Arabic is now {{يعاني عجزاً مالياً}}.

rows.item: “is” as a main verb ({{تعد الترجمة تخصصاً مثيراً للاهتمام}}); stative sentences: the verb “to be” as the main verb (copula, {{ربط}}); Ali is a soldier = {{علي جندي}}; will = {{سـ}}; are = {{تعتبر}} / {{تعد}}
rows.note: Kept as: Arabic normally leaves out “is” and “are” in the present, with {{تُعدّ الترجمة مجالاً شائقاً}} as an option for formal writing.

rows.item: Further grammar notes: “He could” as past ({{استطاع}}) or future ({{كان بإمكانه}}); non-stative sentences, transitive and intransitive verbs, the predicate, prepositional phrases ({{شبه جملة}}), Ali killed the snake, {{قتلت مخاوفي}}, a bare verb as a command (take, move, be); adjectives versus adverbs (high, fast, arrived, flew)
rows.note: Too technical for beginners.

rows.item: Strategy: literal translation, which includes idiomatic translation; it usually fails; key word = {{كلمات دالة}}, not {{كلمات مفتاحية}}
rows.note: Kept as the first strategy; the handbook says the choice between {{كلمة مفتاحية}} and {{كلمة دالّة}} depends on the field.

rows.item: Kick the bucket = {{يموت كالحقير}}; kick the chair = {{انتحر}}
rows.note: The Arabic glosses could not be verified; Chapter 6, Step 1 describes the idiom as informal and humorous.

rows.item: Strategy: functional translation, the translation of equivalents; spill the beans = {{يفشي السر}}; mark my words

rows.item: Strategy: cultural substitution; They are like Romeo and Juliet = {{هما كقيس وليلى}}

rows.item: Strategy: addition, used from English into Arabic because Arabic is a language of elaboration ({{اسهاب}})
rows.note: Uses the Arabic word {{الإطناب}}, and adds the example _the Fed_ = {{مجلس الاحتياطي الفيدرالي الأمريكي}}.

rows.item: Strategy: omission, used from Arabic into English, to be polite; {{شجاع ومغوار}} = brave or quite brave
rows.note: The example is now “very brave”, and politeness is described as avoiding words that would offend the reader.

rows.item: Strategy: explanatory translation, the last option, for cultural and technical words such as {{الصدقة}}, {{الزكاة}}, {{العدة}}, {{الحرمان}}
rows.where: Chapter 14, Step 2; Words to remember, Chapter 14
rows.note: {{الزكاة}} and {{العِدّة}} are kept as examples; {{الصدقة}} and {{الحرمان}} were left out.

rows.item: Key skills: a walking encyclopedia, linguistic repertoire, mental lexicon, bilingual, bicultural, mastery of idiomaticity and phraseology
rows.note: Rewritten as a plain list (two languages, two cultures, curiosity, many idioms); the three special terms were not used.

rows.item: Common challenges: grammar, semantics (choice of words), punctuation and style (formal language or dialect), general versus technical text
rows.note: Kept as four groups of problems, with style linked to register.

rows.item: Table, sentence structure: English SVO versus Arabic VSO; Sam ate the cake
rows.note: The notes marked the subject-first Arabic as wrong (and used “apple”); the handbook calls it correct but less usual and uses {{الكعكة}}.

rows.item: Table, sentence length: short English sentences, long Arabic sentences joined with commas
rows.note: Now says Arabic joins ideas with {{و}}, {{ف}} and {{ثمّ}}, with advice on joining or splitting sentences.

rows.item: Table, language formality: formal versus informal; drama and dialogue are often informal
rows.where: Chapter 4, Step 5; Words to remember, Chapter 4
rows.note: Turned into advice on choosing a dialect (for example in dubbing) and a definition of register.

rows.item: Table, use of synonyms: no two synonyms side by side in English, but Arabic uses them for emphasis
rows.note: Shown with {{شجاعٌ مِغوار}} becoming “very brave”.

rows.item: Types of Arabic: Classical (the Qur’an and pre-Islamic poetry), Standard, Dialectal
rows.where: Chapter 4, Step 5; Words to remember, Chapter 4
rows.note: Classical Arabic is described as the Arabic of the Qur’an and classical poetry, and advice on which type to use was added.

rows.item: Examples: mocktail (a drink without alcohol) and cocktail (a drink with alcohol) in the West
rows.note: Only mocktail is used, translated as {{مشروب مُنعش بلا كحول}}.

rows.item: {{كالمستجير من الرمضاء بالنار}} = out of the frying pan into the fire
rows.note: Kept as a proverb pair; the same proverb is in the Farghal & Shunnaq notes.

rows.item: Tip: fidelity ({{الأمانة}}), being honest and faithful by knowing the meaning of idioms
rows.note: Explained as not adding or removing meaning.

rows.item: Tip: always revise your translation, even the best ones
rows.note: Merged with the advice to read the translation again; Chapter 23 explains how.

rows.item: Tip: make the translation the most faithful, accurate and acceptable
rows.note: Kept as “faithful, accurate and acceptable to the reader”.

rows.item: Tip: translation is rewriting
rows.note: Left out for space.

rows.item: Tip: translation is like a minefield ({{حقل الألغام}}); know what is appropriate in both languages and cultures

rows.item: Tip: prose is stricter, and in poetry you may make creative changes
rows.note: Rewritten: poetry often allows more creative freedom, but informative texts must be exact.

rows.item: Two components: the linguistic level and the external level
rows.note: Written as “look at two levels”, with the linguistic level split into a micro level and a macro level.

rows.item: 1.1.1 Lexical aspects
rows.note: Given as “Words”: vocabulary, terms, figurative language, official titles, cultural expressions and references.

rows.item: 1.1.2 Syntactical aspects
rows.note: Given as “Grammar”, and cohesion is explained as how sentences are linked.

rows.item: 1.1.3 Semantic level
rows.note: Given as “Meaning” and linked to Chapters 6 to 9; speaker’s, sentence and figurative meaning are not listed.

rows.item: 1.1.4 Morphological level
rows.note: Given as “Word forms” (prefixes and suffixes, compounds, acronyms, abbreviations); infixation, blending and clippings are not in that list, although blending is explained in Chapter 17 and clipping in Chapter 21.

rows.item: 1.1.5 Phonological level
rows.note: Given as “Sound”, with where it matters most (poems, slogans, adverts).

rows.item: 1.2.1 Textual level
rows.note: Given as “The text” and linked to Chapter 19; texture and coherence are not listed.

rows.item: 1.2.2 Intertextual level
rows.note: Given as “Other texts” (quotations and allusions); frame-modification, re-modelling and Al-ta’reed were left out as too advanced.

rows.item: 1.2.3 Political and ideological level
rows.note: Given as “Point of view” and linked to Chapter 20.

rows.item: 2. The external level
rows.note: Written as three questions: what background led to the text, who the author is, and how the target culture and audience will affect the translation.

rows.item: 3. Post-translation activity: experience and commentary
rows.note: Added the advice to keep the analysis open while writing the commentary; monitoring, intrinsic and extrinsic managing were left out as too advanced.
